hints: A word can only be glued together from words that are shorter than it. What order of processing guarantees that all its possible pieces are already known?

Sort the words by length. For each word, run a word-break DP using only the words seen so far (all shorter), using a trie of those words to find pieces quickly. If it splits, record it; then add it to the trie.

1. Sort words by length.
  2. For each word w: ok[0] = true; for each start i with ok[i], walk the trie along w from i and set ok[j+1] for every word end at j.
  3. If ok[w.length] is true (and the trie is not empty), add w to the answer.
  4. Insert w into the trie.
  5. Return the answer list.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: For each word, try every way to cut it into pieces recursively and check each piece against a set of all other words.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: Per word, a word-break DP against a hash set of all words (excluding the word itself), checking every substring.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Sort by length; per word, DP + trie walk over only shorter words, then insert the word.

explain: Sample [ice, cream, icecream, ream, creamice, cr], sorted by length: cr, ice, ream, cream, icecream, creamice. cr, ice, ream and cream cannot be split from shorter words (note cream = c+ream fails because c is not a word, and cr+eam fails too). When icecream arrives, ice marks ok[3] and cream from 3 marks ok[8], so it is included; creamice works the same way. Because only strictly shorter words are in the trie, a word can never count itself as one piece, which guarantees two or more pieces. Edge case: the very first (shortest) word must never be reported.
recognize: 'Words that are concatenations of other words in the same list' → sort by length, then word break with a trie of shorter words.
